newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia Gold-Range trading slows buy-backs.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia Gold-Range trading slows buy-backs.

text.p: Australian gold producers appear to be resting on existing forward hedging books as gold continues to trade in a narrow price range.

Following the unwinding of forward sales nearing three million ounces earlier this year such buy-back strategies, whereby producers see opportunities to sell then repurchase gold at a profit, have fallen out of favour.
Next to south Africa, Australian producers are some of the biggest forward sellers in the world, relying on the sales to to fund new mine development and exploration programmes.

However, owing to gold's lack of volatility, compounded by recent gains in the Australian dollar, selling gold either in Japanese yen or U.S. dollars has become highly unattractive, bullion dealers say.
This could change if Australian interest rates are lowered sometime this year, which would likely apply some downward pressure on the Australian dollar, some analysts think.
The weaker the Australian dollar is against other currencies the more attractive it is for producers to sell gold overseas and repatriate the funds.
In the meantime, as long as the gold price is maintained in a narrow band and the Australian dollar hovers near US$0.80, producers will be sitting tight on their forward positions.
Once the gold price does make a move, there are more reasons for the price to go down than up, the analysts note.
On Wednesday, Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said an agreement was near to sell gold from International Monetary Fund vaults to finance loans to the world's poorest nations.
More immediately, the failure of silver to rally from recent price lows is seen as a warning that gold may face the same fate.
"Gold's sort of the same. It's been down to around US$380.00-$380.80 (per oz) and hasn't had much of a bounce," one analyst said.
With plenty of investors holding short positions, a near-term technical test of $380.00 cannot be ruled out, he said.
"If $380.00 holds, you'll see a bounce again. If it doesn't we may see some action on the downside," he added.
In early trading in Europe on Thursday, gold was fetching about $382.40 an ounce.
